papers.title: Mucinous Pancreatic Cysts: A Single-Center Experience Epidemiology, Surveillance, Risk Formulation, Surgery
papers.abstract: Background Mucinous pancreatic cysts demonstrate malignant risk and expanding prevalence. Society guidelines lack underpinning from large, single-center experiences. We describe pancreatic mucinous cyst epidemiology, compare cyst-derived cancers from surveilled vs. non-surveilled cohorts, analyze risk metrics using surveillance and pathologic outcomes, and propose a weighted cancer risk probability score. Methods We conducted a retrospective study of patients at a tertiary metropolitan hospital between January 2006 and December 2025 who were found to have a mucinous pancreatic cyst or cyst-derived cancer on endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). A diagnostic algorithm was used to presumptively diagnose cyst phenotypes; diagnoses were clarified through surveillance and surgery. A preliminary risk classification scheme categorized patients to a risk level based on six binary variables. Cyst-derived cancer (CDCa) were categorized by first encounter or progression from surveillance. Survival analysis of surgical patients was organized by histologic grade and tumor stage. We developed a new malignant progression risk formula that weighted the four most predictive risk metrics: cyst size, main duct phenotype, pancreatic duct dilation, and bile duct dilation. Results 3667 cysts in 3643 patients were analyzed; 2087 (57%) were branch duct and 93 (2.9%) were main duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN), and 79 (2.4%) were mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCN). Unclassifiable cysts (n = 1386, 32%) were analyzed as a primordial branch duct IPMN cohort due to volume and gender equivalents. IPMN-MD were often mislabeled as IPMN-BD during surveillance (43%). Our initial recommended surveillance interval was based on six unweighted metrics: solid nodule, pancreatic or bile duct dilation, main duct involvement, and fluid chemistry. Cyst-derived cancers developed in 8% of mucinous cysts (n = 162). Resection was performed in 184 patients from surveilled (n = 76) and non-surveilled (n = 108) cohorts. Surveilled patients had fewer advanced stage cancers; however, explant pathology was low/moderate dysplasia in 72 resected patients. Kaplan-Meier survival at 5 years was 82% with high-grade dysplasia and T1N0 and 50% for T2N0 and T3N0 lesions. Frequencies of malignant cyst progression were main duct IPMNs (53%), branch duct IPMN (6%), and MCN (5%). Mucinous cyst-derived cancers accounted for 10.7% of all pancreatic adenocarcinomas within our registry. Our logistic regression model achieved a cross-validated area under the ROC of 0.957 (95% CI: 0.944-0.968), with 90% sensitivity at a threshold corresponding to 90% specificity. Conclusion In this longitudinal cohort study, branch duct IPMN was the dominant phenotype, yet main duct IPMN was most likely to progress to malignancy. Surveillance favored early cancer diagnosis yet with low specificity. Post resection survival was excellent and explant pathology revealed lower frequency of nodal disease when compared to PDAC. Risk metric analysis led to a new risk-formulation strategy for patient selection. Our new weighted risk formula offers high predictive accuracy, helping to avoid unnecessary resections.

papers.title: Discovery and Cross-Omic Replication of a Candidate Plasma Proteomic Signature for Anti-TNF Response in Crohn's Disease
papers.abstract: Background and AimsDespite expanding therapeutic options for Crohns disease (CD), treatment selection remains largely empiric. Identifying biomarkers linking inflammatory endotypes to treatment outcomes could inform first-line therapy selection. We sought to identify baseline plasma proteins associated with clinical, biochemical, and endoscopic outcomes in patients with CD receiving anti-TNF therapy. MethodsIn this prospective multicenter cohort, children and young adults with CD initiating infliximab or adalimumab underwent plasma proteomic profiling at baseline and months 3 and 12 using SomaScan v4.1 (7,322 analytes) with deep remission (clinical and endoscopic) as the primary outcome. Rank-based composite correlation analysis identified candidate proteins associated with prespecified treatment outcomes, followed by functional enrichment analyses. Regularized machine learning models were used to derive and evaluate a candidate protein signature. ResultsIn a cohort of 80 participants, mean age 13.7 (SD 3.5) years, 42.5% female, and 90% White, composite rank analysis identified 73 candidate proteins associated with one or more outcomes. Seven candidate proteins (IFNA6, IGHM, MBL2, UBASH3A, REG1A, GABBR2, and NTS) were retained for evaluation. In an independent adult cohort (n=324), models based on whole-blood expression of the seven corresponding genes achieved mean AUPRCs of 0.71 (baseline) and 0.76 (week 14) for the cohort-defined primary response outcome. ConclusionsPlasma proteomic profiling identified a candidate 7 protein signature associated with anti-TNF treatment outcomes in CD. Cross-omic replication demonstrated consistent outcome-associated signals in an independent cohort. Although orthogonal validation of the protein signature is needed, these findings support the potential of proteomic biomarkers to guide biologically informed treatment selection.

papers.title: ColoSTAT: a multiplexed protein blood test to support colonoscopy triage in patients with symptoms of colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: IntroductionMost colorectal cancers (CRCs) are detected after symptomatic presentation in primary care. Because CRC shares symptoms with benign disorders, managing the risk of a missed diagnosis is challenging, and many patients are referred unnecessarily for urgent colonoscopy. As a result, colonoscopy resources cannot keep pace with increasing demand. Simple triage tools that can help prioritise patients for referral are urgently needed. MethodsColoSTAT(R) measures the concentration of five protein biomarkers in a single multiplexed ELISA and was validated in a case-control study enriched for cancer cases. Serum samples from two prospective cross-sectional studies and retrospective biobanked samples were combined into training (300) and validation (200) cohorts, matched for sex, age and clinical diagnosis. Overall, 56% of participants were male, and the median age at sampling was 64 years (range, 28-91 years). The validation cohort was supplemented with an additional 100 serum samples from patients with advanced adenoma (AA) (50.0% female; median age 63 years, range 44-84 years). ResultsCompared with colonoscopy, ColoSTAT(R) detected CRC of all stages with a sensitivity of 89% and a specificity of 51% (90.3% and 54.3% in patients aged 45-84 years). Modelled at an intended-use CRC population prevalence of 4%, the negative predictive value (NPV) was >99% and the positive predictive value (PPV) was approximately 7%. Sensitivity was 90.7% for early-stage and 89.4% for late-stage cancers, and 58% for AA. DiscussionColoSTAT(R) is a potential blood-based aid for the triage of patients with symptoms of CRC. By helping to prioritise symptomatic patients according to their CRC risk, it could improve triage to colonoscopy and support more effective patient management.

papers.title: Real-world adherence to guidelines in acute severe ulcerative colitis: automated assessment using large language models
papers.abstract: Background and AimsAcute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC) is a medical emergency which requires close guideline adherence for optimal outcomes. However, measuring real-world adherence to guidelines and identifying guideline deviations are labor-intensive. We assessed how well a large language model (LLM)-based framework can measure real-world adherence to ASUC guidelines and identify reasons for deviations. MethodsThe retrospective study focused on clinician adherence to the 2025 American College of Gastroenterology guidelines on ASUC. A multi-agent GPT-5 framework first reviewed inpatient health records to confirm ASUC status. Then for each guideline, it assessed whether it was applicable, recommended by consultants, ordered, or executed. This system was benchmarked against manual chart review. The framework was then applied to all the first seven days of all ASUC hospitalizations in 2019-2024 at UCSF. An additional LLM assessed clinical justification of guideline deviations. ResultsThe system reliably recognized ASUC hospitalizations (sensitivity: 0.93) and annotated the guideline cascade (overall accuracy: 0.95, N=60). Across 121 hospitalizations (104 patients), adherence was >80%. Deviations concentrated in deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis (DVTp) and timely rescue therapy. Particularly, DVTp broke down at execution despite appropriate recommendation and ordering, whereas "avoidance" recommendations were followed in practice but seldom explicitly documented. Overall, 62% of non-adherence was unjustified, mostly process delays in DVTp. ConclusionsReal-world ASUC care at a tertiary center was largely guideline-concordant, with actionable gaps in DVT prophylaxis execution and rescue therapy timing. A guideline-constrained LLM system enables scalable monitoring of clinical quality and creates the potential in simultaneously improving clinical care and guidelines.

papers.title: A Whole-Blood Four-Gene Panel Distinguishes Pediatric Crohn's Disease from Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction
papers.abstract: Background and AimsCrohns disease and disorders of gut-brain interaction present with overlapping symptoms, and distinguishing them often requires endoscopy. We assessed whether the whole-blood transcriptome at presentation distinguishes these conditions and reflects disease activity. MethodsIn a prospective two-center cohort, whole-blood RNA sequencing was performed in 425 treatment-naive participants aged 5 to 25 years (112 Crohns disease, 313 disorders of gut-brain interaction). Differential expression was modeled for diagnosis and, within Crohns disease, for the Pediatric Crohns Disease Activity Index. Co-expression modules were integrated with protein-protein interaction networks, and machine learning distilled network genes into a diagnostic panel, evaluated internally and in an independent pediatric cohort. ResultsOf 1,095 diagnosis-associated genes, 377 were also associated with disease activity, all with concordant direction. Five co-expression networks were perturbed, spanning neutrophil degranulation, hemostasis, interferon signaling, and T-cell and cytotoxic lymphocyte programs. A 4-gene panel (PSTPIP2, CLIC4, CACNB4, GZMK) drawn from 4 networks achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of up to 0.96 in held-out samples and up to 0.93 externally, with external specificity and positive predictive value of up to 0.95 and 0.93, respectively. The panel matched or exceeded every single-network panel with fewer genes, and minimally active Crohns disease overlapped transcriptionally with disorders of gut-brain interaction. ConclusionsAt diagnosis, Crohns disease is distinguished from disorders of gut-brain interaction by a systemic signature of neutrophil and platelet activation and lymphocyte depletion that scales with disease activity. A 4-gene whole-blood panel may help prioritize symptomatic children for endoscopy and warrants prospective validation.

papers.title: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies
papers.abstract: ObjectiveBiopsies are examined under the microscope by a pathologist, giving a diagnosis, which guides treatment and predicts prognosis. A shortage of pathologists and increasing workload leads to diagnostic delays, while for duodenal (small intestinal) biopsies, variable diagnostic concordance between pathologists limits accuracy. These challenges have motivated us to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated approach for the automated diagnosis of up to 80% of duodenal biopsies (i.e., most cases of the two most frequent diagnoses: coeliac disease and "normal"). We set out to understand patient, carer and stakeholder views regarding the adoption of such technology. Methods and AnalysisWe conducted mixed-methods stakeholder engagement (February 2024 to June 2026). We ran a national online patients and carers questionnaire (n=231 respondents) and four UK focus-group workshops, one of which additionally captured Likert-scale attitudes1 immediately before and after a structured educational session (n=34 matched pairs). Healthcare professionals completed an online questionnaire (n=37) and took part in a structured workshop. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively; free-text and workshop data were analysed thematically and triangulated across all sources. ResultsMost patients and carers supported AI-reliant diagnosis (68.4%) and would strongly trust systems with formal regulatory approval (66.7%). Most wanted to be informed if AI was used (73.6%), but only 52.4% felt explicit permission was necessary. Qualitative themes centred on clear and available evidence of accuracy, human oversight, transparent communication and clear terminology, with the term machine learning being preferred to artificial intelligence. Agreement ( agree or strongly agree combined) with statements relating to trust, acceptance and perceived benefit of AI was significantly higher after a structured educational session (38.2% to 67.6%, 85.3% to 97.1%, and 52.9% to 97.1% respectively; all p[≤]0.003). Healthcare professionals favoured an AI assistant model over full automation, citing the need for validation, explainability, data governance and workflow integration. Patients also preferred some level of human oversight. ConclusionPatients and healthcare professionals are cautiously supportive of AI-assisted diagnosis of duodenal biopsies, conditional upon demonstration of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication. Attitudes towards AI-assisted diagnosis were more favourable after structured explanation. Key MessagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSVery little is known about patients, carers or healthcare professionals views about the automation of diagnosis in pathology, using AI-based software solutions. What this study adds{Rightarrow} This is the first study to investigate patient, carer and healthcare professional attitudes specifically to AI-mediated duodenal biopsy diagnosis. Around two-thirds of respondents supported AI-assisted diagnosis, contingent upon clear and available evidence of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication, together with appropriate regulatory approval of the technology. {Rightarrow}Attitudes were markedly more favourable after a single structured educational session: agreement that AI could improve duodenal biopsy diagnosis nearly doubled and trust in healthcare AI rose substantially, suggesting that public views of AI in diagnosis can be influenced by clear explanation. {Rightarrow}Patients and healthcare professionals both favour some ongoing level of human oversight of any AI-based diagnostic approach. How this study might affect research, practice or policy{Rightarrow} Our study suggests that a phased, AI-assistant-first deployment model with defined validation and audit checkpoints would be most readily acceptable when introducing diagnostic AI into histopathology. {Rightarrow}It indicates that appropriate information and education, for example, a patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) session, can increase trust in AI in healthcare. {Rightarrow}It shows that patients and the public are more trusting of technology for which the term machine learning is used, rather than artificial intelligence (AI). {Rightarrow}It offers a stakeholder-engagement template for use by others introducing AI-based diagnostics.

papers.title: Accurate Prediction of Hepatic Disease Severity in MASLD Using a Learned Phenotype
papers.abstract: Background & AimsMost prognostic models for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) target prespecified hepatic endpoints, potentially limiting attainable accuracy. We developed and externally validated a model that learns the future hepatic phenotype most reliably predictable from baseline clinical characteristics. MethodsWe analyzed 332 HALO-MASLD participants (456 follow-up observations). Sparse Canonical Outcome REgression (SCORE) learned a weighted phenotype from eight hepatic measures, coupled with broken adaptive ridge regression using 99 baseline predictor columns. Participant-level nested five-fold cross-validation compared prediction of the learned phenotype with future liver stiffness measurement (LSM), controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), and FIB-4 benchmarks. Models were externally validated without refitting in the independent NIDDK NAFLD Adult Database 2 cohort (520 participants, 732 follow-up observations). Biological validity and bootstrap stability were also assessed. ResultsThe learned phenotype emphasized lower platelet count and higher bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and LSM. In HALO, predictive correlation was r = 0.860 (95% CI [0.824, 0.896]) and predictive R2 = 0.671, versus r = 0.763 for LSM and r = 0.469 for CAP predicted from all baseline variables. All six prespecified comparisons remained significant after Holm correction (pHolm < 0.05). The phenotype correlated with MRE stiffness ({rho} = 0.694) and biopsy fibrosis stage ({rho} = 0.567), and was higher with imaging evidence of portal hypertension (p < 0.001). Bootstrap relearning yielded mean phenotype correlation 0.947. In NIDDK, predictive correlation was r = 0.836 (95% CI [0.805, 0.863]; predictive R2 = 0.680), and associations with fibrosis and portal hypertension replicated. ConclusionsLearning the prediction target produced a sparse, clinically interpretable hepatic phenotype more accurately predicted than conventional longitudinal MASLD endpoints in both cohorts. The resulting LIFT-MASLD model is available at https://liftmasld.github.io.

papers.title: Molecular age of Barrett's esophagus indicates onset often occurs decades before diagnosis
papers.abstract: BackgroundTimely identification of Barretts esophagus (BE) is crucial for early esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) detection. Screening is recommended from age 50 in individuals with additional risk factors, but biological BE onset age remains unknown. ObjectiveEstimate biological BE onset age and duration before clinical diagnosis (dwell time). DesignWe applied a BE epigenetic clock to 61 samples from 41 patients in a population-representative Northern Ireland cohort and 164 samples from 140 patients in an independent UK cohort. BE dwell times were compared between patients with concurrent dysplasia/EAC and age- and sex-matched non-dysplastic BE controls in these cross-sectional studies. In a longitudinal cohort, pre-progression biopsies from 31 future high-grade dysplasia (HGD)/EAC progressors were compared with 35 non-progressors. ResultsMedian estimated BE onset ages in the cross-sectional cohorts were 29.5 (IQR=22.5-45.8) and 29.3 (IQR=20.4-39.0) years, respectively. These estimates were further supported by independent epidemiologic modeling of age-specific BE prevalence data from more than 70,000 BE cases. Estimated dwell times were longer in patients with concurrent dysplasia (median difference 14.3 years; p=0.0042) or EAC (12.5 years; p=0.0002) than matched non-dysplastic BE controls. Dwell time exceeding 19.8 years was associated with higher odds of HGD/EAC progression (OR=12.1, 95% CI 3.7-47.5; p=9.96 x 10-). ConclusionBE may arise decades before diagnosis. Although these findings do not justify lowering screening age, they suggest one-time screening from age 50 years may detect existing high-risk BE. Further modeling is warranted to evaluate implications for population-based screening, alongside prospective validation of epigenetic tissue age for progression risk stratification. Key MessagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSIncreasing patient age is a major clinical risk factor for both esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) and its precursor lesion, Barretts esophagus (BE), but the biological age or dwell time of BE before diagnosis cannot be directly measured clinically, limiting our understanding of BE onset timing and past disease evolution. What this study addsUsing a methylation-based molecular clock model applied to 294 tissue samples, we estimated that the median age of onset of BE is approximately 30 years old in 3 independent UK cohorts with BE. We found substantial interpatient variability in estimated BE onset age, significantly older BE tissue age in patients with adjacent EAC or dysplasia, and 12-fold higher odds of HGD/EAC progression for patients with older BE tissue age in a prospectively followed cohort. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThese findings suggest that BE may arise decades before clinical diagnosis, providing a prolonged window for EAC prevention and supporting further investigation of one-time screening from age 50 to identify existing high-risk BE, rather than broadly lowering screening ages. Molecular estimates of BE tissue age may improve computational models of BE natural history and inform future biomarkers for neoplastic progression risk stratification, warranting further modeling and prospective validation to assess their potential utility in personalized screening and surveillance strategies.

papers.title: Genome-wide association meta-analysis of atrophic gastritis reveals anti H. pylori IgG serostatus dependent associations and genetic overlap with gastric cancer
papers.abstract: BackgroundAtrophic gastritis (AG), characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa and glandular atrophy, is an established precursor of gastric cancer (GC) and contributes to iron-deficiency anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and pernicious anemia. Although Helicobacter pylori infection is a major environmental determinant, not all infected individuals develop AG or GC, suggesting that host genetic factors influence susceptibility to AG and severe atrophic gastritis (SAG). Previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of AG have been limited in size and have not adequately compared anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus strata, leaving potential genetic heterogeneity unresolved. MethodsWe performed GWAS meta-analyses of AG and SAG, stratified by anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus, involving 214,747 Japanese participants: 75,074 in the discovery phase and 139,673 in the replication phase. Subsequent analyses included genotype-by-serostatus interactions, HLA allele and ABO blood group associations, genome-wide genetic correlations, multi-trait analysis, local genetic correlations, and structural equation modeling. In addition, cross-ancestry meta-analyses were performed using chronic gastritis GWAS data from FinnGen, UK Biobank, and the Million Veteran Program, comprising 1,357,053 participants. ResultsAcross six Japanese GWAS meta-analyses, we identified genome-wide significant associations at 17 genomic regions. Strong associations with seropositive AG/SAG were observed at previously reported GC susceptibility loci, including PSCA and MUC1/MTX1, whereas the MHC class II region showed predominant associations with seronegative AG/SAG. FAP, CCR6, and ATP4A were also found to be associated with seronegative SAG. The identified regions included previously reported GC susceptibility regions MUC1/MTX1, PRKAA1/PTGER4, PSCA, ABO, and MHC. Associations at PSCA and MUC1/MTX1 were replicated at a genome-wide significance level, supporting a shared genetic basis between AG/SAG and GC. Additional AG-associated candidate regions included BMP2, CCDC80, LRRC34, CPEB4, PGC/FRS3, and LMTK2, implicating epithelial regulation, immune responses, transcriptional regulation, and differentiation. A positive genotype-by-serostatus interaction for SAG was observed at MUC1/MTX1. HLA class II alleles, including HLA-DRB1*15:01 and HLA-DQB1*06:02, showed associations with seronegative AG/SAG. The LDSC genetic correlation between AG and GC was 0.529, and the MTAG estimated Omega correlation was 0.694. Local genetic correlation analysis and structural equation modeling further supported shared genetic components. Cross-ancestry integration of seronegative SAG with external chronic gastritis GWAS data identified an additional association at TPTEP1. ConclusionsOur findings characterize the genetic heterogeneity of serologically defined AG/SAG according to anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus. They highlight epithelial and mucus barrier-related pathways in seropositive AG/SAG and immune-related pathways in seronegative cases, while also providing evidence of a shared genetic basis between AG and GC. Together, these results clarify the genetic basis of a GC precursor and are consistent with a continuum from chronic inflammation through atrophy to carcinogenesis. These insights may inform prevention strategies and personalized management of the diverse health consequences of AG.

papers.title: Saccharomyces boulardii as Adjunctive Therapy in Helicobacter pylori Eradication: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: BackgroundHelicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection remains highly prevalent in Iran, where high antibiotic resistance can limit eradication efficacy. Saccharomyces boulardii (S. boulardii) may improve eradication and treatment tolerability, although evidence remains inconsistent. This trial evaluated adjunctive S. boulardii in a high-prevalence, high-resistance setting. MethodsIn this randomized, single-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 218 H. pylori-positive adults received 14 days of PPI, bismuth, amoxicillin, and clarithromycin (P-BAC) plus either S. boulardii (250 mg twice daily) or placebo. The primary outcome was H. pylori eradication assessed 30 days after treatment by stool antigen testing, analyzed by intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) principles. Treatment-related adverse events were secondary outcomes. Trial registration: Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials, IRCT20230827059280N1. ResultsIn the PP analysis, eradication was lower with S. boulardii than placebo (65.0% vs. 76.5%; RR = 0.849, 95% CI: 0.709-1.018), with a similar pattern in the ITT analysis (59.6% vs. 68.8%; RR = 0.867, 95% CI: 0.710-1.058). Neither analysis showed a statistically significant difference. Overall adverse events were significantly less frequent with S. boulardii (44.0% vs. 68.4%; RR = 0.644, 95% CI: 0.497-0.834; P < 0.001), with lower rates of bloating (4.0% vs. 23.5%; adjusted P < 0.001) and epigastric pain (4.0% vs. 14.3%; adjusted P = 0.041). ConclusionAdjunctive S. boulardii did not significantly improve H. pylori eradication with 14-day P-BAC therapy. However, it significantly reduced adverse events, particularly bloating and epigastric pain. Further multicenter trials incorporating individualized susceptibility testing are warranted.

papers.title: Symptom variability and treatment response in pernicious anaemia: a longitudinal daily symptom tracking study
papers.abstract: Pernicious Anaemia is an autoimmune-mediated disorder of vitamin B12 absorption, managed using fixed-interval vitamin B12 replacement regimens. Despite treatment, many patients report persistent or recurrent symptoms, suggesting substantial inter-individual variability in treatment response. More tailored approaches may therefore be needed to reduce symptom burden and improve quality of life. This prospective observational study used high-frequency longitudinal digital symptom monitoring to characterise symptom dynamics and heterogeneity in treatment response. UK adults with pernicious anaemia, recruited via the Pernicious Anaemia Society, self-reported daily symptoms (severity 0-10) and vitamin B12 treatments over three months. Analyses quantified within- and between-person variability, injection-aligned symptom response kinetics, and differences in treatment response by injection frequency. Sixty-eight participants were included in the longitudinal analyses, providing >5,100 person-days of symptom data over a mean of 76 days (SD 28). Most symptom variance was attributable to stable between-person differences (ICC range, 0.58-0.80), indicating the persistence of individual symptom phenotypes. Vitamin B12 injections were followed by rapid symptom improvement, although magnitude and timing varied markedly by symptom domain. Seventy-one percent of participants were classified as responders for composite symptom burden (median 4.65 to 2.36; p<0.001), while 29% showed no meaningful multisystem improvement (3.59 to 3.58; p=0.63). Cognitive symptoms improved earliest, typically within 24-72 hours; fatigue and pain responses peaked at 3-5 days, and neuro-sensory symptoms at 4-6 days. Responses clustered within individuals, indicating distinct responder phenotypes. Overall symptom burden improved most among participants receiving monthly injections, whereas those injecting weekly or more often had higher pre-injection burden and smaller improvements. These findings suggest that fixed-interval vitamin B12 replacement may not adequately reflect individual variation in symptom recurrence and treatment response. High-frequency digital symptom monitoring may provide a practical framework for characterising these patterns and for evaluating more individualised, symptom-guided vitamin B12 management. Author SummaryPernicious anaemia is a lifelong autoimmune condition that prevents the body from properly absorbing vitamin B12. Although regular vitamin B12 injections are used to treat the condition, many people continue to experience symptoms between injections and it is unclear why treatment works better for some people than others. We asked 68 people with pernicious anaemia to record their symptoms and vitamin B12 treatments every day for up to three months. This allowed us to examine how symptoms changed over time and around individual injections. We found that symptoms often improved after vitamin B12 injections, but the size and timing of improvement varied considerably between people and between different symptoms. Some participants showed improvement across many symptoms, while others showed little change. We also found that symptoms often returned between injections, even in people receiving long-term treatment. Our findings show how frequent digital symptom tracking can reveal patterns that may be missed during short clinical appointments. In the future, this approach could help clinicians and researchers evaluate whether vitamin B12 treatment can be better tailored to an individuals symptoms and treatment response.

papers.title: Histological and molecular responses to pemafibrate in MASLD with hypertriglyceridemia: the CLARITY study
papers.abstract: Background & AimsThe histological effects and underlying molecular responses to pemafibrate in MASLD remain poorly defined. We investigated longitudinal histological changes and cell-type-specific molecular responses in patients with MASLD and hypertriglyceridemia. MethodsIn the prospective, single-arm CLARITY study, 33 patients with MASLD and hypertriglyceridemia received pemafibrate (0.2 mg/day) and underwent paired liver biopsies at baseline and 52 weeks. Primary outcomes were changes in fibrosis stage and NAFLD activity score (NAS). Complementary analyses included dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, pooled liver single-nucleus RNA sequencing, paired hepatic qPCR, and circulating proteomics. An external mouse transcriptomic dataset was analysed to investigate the contribution of hepatocyte PPAR. ResultsFibrosis stage improved in 16 of 33 patients (48.5%), remained unchanged in 16, and worsened in one; 13 patients (39.4%) achieved fibrosis improvement without NAS worsening. Both fibrosis stage and NAS decreased significantly (P<0.001 and P=0.003, respectively). ALT decreased from 64 to 28 U/L and triglycerides from 169 to 90 mg/dL (both P<0.001), without significant changes in body weight or DXA-derived body composition. Single-nucleus profiling revealed increased hepatocyte PPAR/fatty acid oxidation-associated transcriptional scores and reduced fibrogenic extracellular matrix and inflammatory programmes in HSCs/fibroblasts and macrophages/Kupffer cells, respectively. Paired hepatic qPCR confirmed reductions in COL1A1, THBS2, DCN, TIMP1 and TREM2, together with increased HMGCS2. Circulating proteomics revealed increased FGF21 and decreased DCN, IL1B, and CXCL8 levels. In external mouse data, selected metabolic transcriptional responses were attenuated by hepatocyte-specific PPAR deletion. ConclusionsPemafibrate treatment was associated with histological improvement and coordinated, cell-type-specific metabolic and fibro-inflammatory remodelling in MASLD with hypertriglyceridemia. Convergent human tissue and circulating molecular findings, supported by external genetic evidence, implicate hepatocyte PPAR-related pathways in these responses. Impact and implicationsIn patients with MASLD and hypertriglyceridemia, pemafibrate treatment was associated with improved fibrosis and disease activity on paired liver biopsies. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing identified increased expression of selected fatty acid oxidation genes in hepatocytes and reduced matrix-related and inflammatory gene expression in hepatic stellate cells and macrophages, respectively. Paired hepatic qPCR in 28 patients and circulating proteomics supported key molecular findings, including reduced collagen-related gene expression and increased circulating FGF21. These findings connect histological improvement with cell-specific hepatic responses and support controlled evaluation of pemafibrate as a potential treatment for MASLD with hypertriglyceridemia.

papers.title: Stool host transcriptome reveals gut epithelial cell states and immune dynamics for gastrointestinal diagnosis and monitoring
papers.abstract: Gastrointestinal diagnosis and monitoring rely on colonoscopy, which requires anesthesia and a long wait, and non-invasive alternatives are lacking. Here we show that whole-transcriptome sequencing of stool host RNA, recovering a median of 6,300 protein-coding genes across 285 libraries spanning colorectal cancer (CRC) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), precancerous lesions (APL), and normal samples, reads a census of the cells shed into the lumen. In normal samples, epithelium supplies 81% and immune cells supply 11% of stool host mRNA transcripts; the immune cells share rises in CRC and IBD, and B- and T-cell receptor clonotypes rise with it. In this work, we show that CRC, IBD, and normal samples carry distinct transcriptome profiles, which a three-class model separates with an area under the curve of 0.94-0.96, and that within inflammatory bowel disease a 15-gene neutrophil score tracks endoscopic activity better than fecal calprotectin in the same stool.

papers.title: Selective Bacteroidota Depletion but Not Global Microbiome Differences in Short Bowel Syndrome on Fiber-Free Enteral Nutrition
papers.abstract: Intestinal dysbiosis in pediatric short bowel syndrome (SBS) is associated with poor growth, but the factors that are driving this dysbiosis remain unclear. Prior studies suggest that parenteral nutrition (PN) dependence and remnant intestinal anatomy are correlated with dysbiosis. However, these studies often compared SBS patients to healthy controls, making it difficult to distinguish SBS-specific factors from alterations due to differences in diet, namely the consumption of enteral nutrition with complex composition and exposure to dietary fiber. In this preliminary report from the GREENBEANS study, we examined baseline stool shotgun metagenomic profiles from 10 SBS patients and 13 non-SBS controls receiving fiber-free enteral nutrition. Alpha diversity did not differ significantly between groups by richness or Shannon diversity. Beta diversity showed minimal separation by Bray-Curtis distance and modest separation in Jaccard distance. Differential abundance analysis identified depletion of Bacteroidota in SBS. Compared to control patients also receiving fiber-free enteral nutrition, SBS was associated with only a small global difference in the gut microbiome, suggesting that diet, and not anatomy as previously assumed, is the predominant determinant of gut microbiome structure. This suggests that the inclusion of complex substrates, such as dietary fiber, in enteral nutrition, may be a modality to prevent the development of a dysbiotic microbiome in patients with SBS. What is known/What is newO_ST_ABSWhat is knownC_ST_ABSO_LIChildren with short bowel syndrome (SBS) often demonstrate intestinal dysbiosis characterized by reduced microbial diversity and enrichment of Proteobacteria/Enterobacteriaceae compared with healthy controls. C_LIO_LIDysbiosis in SBS is associated with increased PN dependence and poor growth outcomes. C_LIO_LIThe relative contribution of various SBS-associated factors to this dysbiosis remains unclear because prior studies generally used healthy control subjects. C_LI What is newO_LISBS-specific differences while on fiber-free enteral nutrition were driven primarily by selective depletion of Bacteroidota anaerobes rather than broad Proteobacteria expansion. C_LIO_LISBS was associated with only a modest global microbiome separation from non-SBS controls when both were receiving fiber-free enteral nutrition, suggesting that the lack of dietary fiber, rather than the alteration of intestinal anatomy or other SBS-specific factors, may be a major factor in the development of the SBS-associated dysbiosis found in prior studies. C_LIO_LIOur findings shift attention from fixed anatomic factors alone towards potentially modifiable dietary contributors in SBS-associated dysbiosis, including enteral substrate complexity and dietary fiber exposure. papers.title: Interval colorectal cancer risk by haemoglobin concentration in Australia's National Bowel Cancer Screening Program
papers.abstract: BackgroundInterval colorectal cancers (CRCs) are an important measure of screening performance. We assessed interval CRC risk after negative faecal immunochemical testing (FIT), its association with faecal haemoglobin (f-Hb) concentration, and differences by age and sex in Australia s National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (NBCSP). MethodsWe conducted a population-based retrospective cohort study linking Queensland screening and cancer registry records for NBCSP participants aged 50-74 years screened in 2018-2022. Eligible episodes had f-Hb below 20 ug/g in both samples. We excluded episodes with CRC diagnosed on or before follow-up start. Follow-up ended at CRC, the next screening episode, death, 24 months, or December 31, 2023. We estimated adjusted cause-specific hazard ratios (HRs), accounting for repeated episodes within participants, and cumulative incidence with death and subsequent screening as competing events. FindingsAmong 1,083,149 negative screening episodes from 700,734 participants, 586 interval CRCs occurred over 2,056,405 person-years. The incidence rate was 28.5 per 100,000 person-years, and 24-month cumulative incidence was 57.6 per 100,000 episodes (95% CI 53.1-62.5). Risk increased with age and was higher in males (adjusted HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.08-1.50). The complete-case quantitative cohort included 326,931 episodes and 138 cancers. Compared with maximum f-Hb of 0-5 ug/g, concentrations >15-<20 ug/g were associated with an adjusted HR of 14.93 (9.02-24.70). Corresponding 24-month risks were 35.7 (28.5-44.7) and 504.5 (323.4-787.0) per 100,000 episodes. Higher negative-range f-Hb concentrations were more common in older participants and males. The quantitative cohort showed no clear sex difference after adjustment for f-Hb. InterpretationCRC risk varies substantially among people with a negative screening result. Quantitative F-Hb levels may help identify who is at higher risk of interval CRC. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and assess the benefits, harms and costs of changing screening intervals. Research in contextO_ST_ABSResearch in contextC_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyWe searched PubMed October 2026, for Australian studies and international systematic reviews and meta-analyses, using combinations of "colorectal", "bowel", "interval cancer", "interval cancers", "interval colorectal", "negative FIT", "faecal haemoglobin", "fecal hemoglobin", "faecal immunochemical", and "fecal immunochemical", combined with "Australia", "Australian", "systematic review", or "meta-analysis". Additional searches examined international cohort studies published from January 1, 2020, to October 25, 2026. Australian national monitoring and a study in Western Australia showed that interval CRC was uncommon but more frequent among males and older participants. Both analyses were based on the 2018 screening cohort, before biennial screening had been fully implemented for all eligible people aged 50-74 years. Neither examined interval CRC risk across the negative f-Hb range. International reviews documented substantial variation in interval CRC incidence between screening programmes. More recent Danish and Dutch cohort studies showed that higher f-Hb concentrations below the positivity threshold were associated with greater interval CRC risk, including after successive negative screening rounds. A dose-response meta-analysis of 13 studies supported the prognostic value of negative-range f-Hb, but combined evidence on interval cancers, cancers detected at subsequent screening, and adenomas. These outcomes do not provide interchangeable estimates of risk before the next screen. The evidence therefore supported further investigation of quantitative f-Hb, but did not establish concentration-specific interval CRC risks for the NBCSPs two-sample protocol and 20 {micro}g/g positivity threshold. Added value of this studyThis study extends Australian evidence through longitudinal linkage of Queensland screening and cancer registry records from 2018-2022, including repeated screening episodes from more than 700,000 participants. It estimates interval CRC risk overall and by age and sex, and examines how that risk varies within the negative f-Hb range. Follow-up ended at the next screening episode, allowing interval cancers to be distinguished from cancers detected at later screening. The quantitative analysis showed a substantial concentration gradient in both relative and absolute risk, despite all included results being classified as negative. By providing absolute risks within the Australian screening setting, the study offers evidence directly relevant to evaluating whether participants with different negative f-Hb concentrations could benefit from different screening intervals. Implications of all the available evidenceA negative FIT result provides reassurance, but does not indicate the same level of interval CRC risk for every participant. Together, the international evidence and our findings support evaluating screening strategies that use quantitative f-Hb rather than relying solely on a positive or negative result in the Australian program. They do not establish which screening intervals or thresholds should be adopted. Further evaluation should determine whether tailoring screening reduces interval cancers and advanced disease without disproportionate increases in colonoscopy use, harms, or inequalities in access and outcomes.

papers.title: Detection of Human Bocavirus in Stool Samples Collected During an Outbreak of Acute Gastroenteritis in Children in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil
papers.abstract: Introduction: This study investigated human bocavirus (HBoV) in samples obtained during an outbreak of acute gastroenteritis (AGE) among children in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil. AGE is characterized by symptoms including diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and fever and may require hospitalization in severe cases. Methods: A total of 131 stool samples collected from children hospitalized with AGE at a hospital in Salvador, Bahia, were analyzed. HBoV was detected using nested polymerase chain reaction (nested PCR). Positive samples were sequenced and inoculated into Vero cell cultures, followed by sodium dodecyl sulfate- polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and Western blotting. Results: Of the 131 samples analyzed, 13 tested positive for HBoV. Children aged 0-4 years were the most affected by AGE and showed the highest frequency of HBoV detection. HBoV was successfully cultured in Vero cells, representing a novel finding reported in this study. Subsequent SDS-PAGE and Western blot analyses revealed protein bands suggestive of HBoV structural proteins. Conclusion: This study highlights the need for accurate diagnostic methods and preventive strategies to control the spread of HBoV and other pathogens associated with gastroenteritis in pediatric populations.

papers.title: IBDex: A Frozen Patient-Scale Atlas for Bulk Transcriptomics in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: Background & AimsBulk mucosal RNA sequencing in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is analyzed one cohort at a time, so each study rebuilds its own molecular scale. We aimed to build a frozen atlas that new cohorts could use without retraining. MethodsWe built IBDex from 3,168 intestinal biopsies from 1,680 patients with Crohns disease, ulcerative colitis or no IBD, drawn from four cohorts. Patients were kept within a single training, validation or test partition. A tissue-aware conditional variational autoencoder with adversarial suppression of cohort identity was trained on a 3,000-gene interface. The scaling, encoder, decoder, pathway basis and phenotype directions were then frozen. Phenotype-anchored counterfactual perturbation (PACP) produced anatomy-conditioned gene-response maps. We tested the atlas without parameter updates in three unseen IBD cohorts, a longitudinal olamkicept trial, and cohorts with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) or colorectal cancer (CRC). ResultsIn held-out data, dataset identity fell to near chance (balanced accuracy 0.307 vs 0.250). Anatomy, diagnosis and inflammation remained recoverable (inflammation AUC 0.82). Marginal differential expression conflated inflammation and disease state ({rho} = 0.834). PACP separated them ({rho} = -0.161), with inflammation driven by TNF-NF-{kappa}B, and disease state by proliferative, type I interferon and metabolic programs. In 93 patients in combined endoscopic and histological remission, inflammation approached controls (AUC 0.58), but disease state stayed displaced (AUC 0.725, P = 1.8 x 10{square}1{square}). The frozen atlas recovered clinical, single-cell-defined and disease-behavior structure in unseen cohorts. It also tracked responder trajectories during olamkicept therapy and separated PSC (patient-level AUC 0.794) and CRC (AUC 0.938- 1.000). Where de novo differential expression became unreliable, transferred response maps stayed reproducible ({rho} [≥] 0.89). ConclusionsIBDex turns historical bulk biopsy data into a reusable reference. It shows that deep remission moves inflammation toward control levels but leaves a persistent molecular disease state.

papers.title: Understanding Psychological Health in Adults with Irritable Bowel Syndrome: A Cross-Sectional Study Using the All of Us Research Program
papers.abstract: BackgroundPsychological health is an important aspect of health and well-being among adults with irritable bowel syndrome, yet the interrelationships among individual vulnerabilities, social experiences, perceived stress, and psychological health outcomes remain poorly understood. ObjectiveTo characterize psychological health and examine direct and indirect associations of childhood adversity and adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptoms within an adapted Stress Process Model. DesignCross-sectional secondary analysis. SettingThe United States All of Us Research Program. Participants2,417 adults with electronic health record-documented irritable bowel syndrome and complete data on the primary analysis variables and covariates. MethodsSeparate structural equation models examined childhood adversity and adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptoms in relation to perceived stress, anxiety and depressive symptoms, and positive psychological well-being, with loneliness and perceived social support as psychosocial pathways. Models adjusted for sociodemographic and social-context factors. ResultsThe median age was 54.39 years; 80.7% were female and 84.4% were White. Moderate-to-high perceived stress was reported by 56.2%, at least moderate anxiety symptoms by 21.0%, and at least moderate depressive symptoms by 24.3%. Higher ACE-8 scores were associated with greater perceived stress, anxiety symptoms, and depressive symptoms and lower psychological well-being ({beta} = 0.063, 0.089, 0.116, and -0.100, respectively); corresponding associations for higher ASRS-6 scores were {beta} = 0.299, 0.355, 0.390, and -0.260. Loneliness-specific indirect associations were positive for perceived stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms (ACE-8: {beta} = 0.023-0.034; ASRS-6: {beta} = 0.043-0.075) and negative for psychological well-being (ACE-8: {beta} = -0.039; ASRS-6: {beta} = -0.089; all p < .001). Social support-specific indirect associations were not significant in the ACE-8 model and were small and significant only for anxiety and depression in the ASRS-6 model ({beta} = 0.003-0.004). ConclusionsPsychological health among adults with irritable bowel syndrome was associated with interconnected individual and social factors within an adapted Stress Process Model. Childhood adversity and adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptoms showed direct and indirect associations with psychological health, with loneliness emerging as the most consistent social factor. These findings support prospective investigation of individual vulnerabilities and social experiences in psychological health. The cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causal mediation. What is already knownO_LIPsychological distress is common in adults with irritable bowel syndrome. C_LIO_LILoneliness and perceived social support describe distinct social experiences. C_LI What this paper addsO_LIChildhood adversity and adult attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity symptom burden were linked to psychological health. C_LIO_LILoneliness was associated with distress and lower psychological well-being. C_LI

papers.title: Detection and Characterization of Human Bocavirus in Stool Samples from an Acute Gastroenteritis Outbreak in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, in 2024.
papers.abstract: IntroductionAcute gastroenteritis (AGE) is a global public health problem and a major cause of mortality in low- and lower-middle-income countries. Human bocavirus (HBoV) is among the viral agents associated with this condition. Therefore, investigating the presence of HBoV in cases of AGE in Salvador, Bahia, as well as its prevalence and circulating strains, is important. ObjectiveTo investigate the occurrence of HBoV infection during an AGE outbreak in Salvador. MethodsA total of 178 samples were analyzed for HBoV using nested polymerase chain reaction (nested PCR), and the amplification products were visualized by agarose gel electrophoresis. HBoV was detected in 5.7% of the samples analyzed. ConclusionThis study contributes to the understanding of HBoV epidemiology as a secondary agent associated with acute gastroenteritis during a norovirus outbreak in Salvador. Continued investigation and identification of the etiological agents involved in outbreaks are essential for evaluating the causes of AGE. These findings also highlight the need for broader diagnostic approaches and the importance of phylogenetic analysis for monitoring and controlling viral infections.

papers.title: Adenovirus as a Causative Agent of an Acute Gastroenteritis Outbreak in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil.
papers.abstract: IntroductionAcute gastroenteritis (AGE) is a cause of childhood morbidity and may be associated with human adenovirus (HAdV) infection. This study aimed to investigate the occurrence of HAdV in fecal samples from children with AGE in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, as well as to molecularly characterize the identified strains and evaluate their cytopathic effects in cell culture. MethodsA total of 131 samples were analyzed using the nested polymerase chain reaction (Nested-PCR) technique. Molecular characterization was performed through Sanger sequencing and phylogenetic analysis, while Vero cell cultures were used to investigate the occurrence of cytopathic effects. ResultsOf the samples analyzed, 13 (9.9%) tested positive for HAdV, while 118 (90.1%) were negative. The highest detection frequency was observed in children aged three years or younger, particularly those under one year of age. Phylogenetic analysis identified variants related to HAdV-F41 and HAdV-B3, revealing genetic differences and distinct clustering patterns compared with reference sequences. In cell culture, cytopathic effects were observed four days after inoculation, although further analyses are required to confirm productive viral replication. ConclusionThese findings demonstrate the presence of HAdV in the samples studied and contribute to understanding its genetic diversity and circulation in Salvador, highlighting the importance of epidemiological surveillance and further studies on its role in the etiology of childhood AGE.

papers.title: Protracted copy number alteration evolution in Barrett's oesophagus leading to oesophageal cancer
papers.abstract: Detection of copy number alterations (CNAs) in Barretts oesophagus (BO) predicts oesophageal adenocarcinoma (OAC) risk. When CNAs first occur is unknown. Here we show that CNAs typically form in BO many decades prior to first clinical detection of BO or cancer, and often during childhood. Using a novel molecular clock analysis, we analysed spatiotemporal longitudinal whole genome data from 80 individuals within BO surveillance. Chr 9p loss of heterozygosity (LOH) tended to be the first CNA event typically occurring at age 10-30 years. Genome doubling (GD) also typically originated multiple decades prior to cancer develop. Patients who progressed to OAC had an enrichment of CNAs late in life. CNA rate was more predictive of cancer risk than CNA burden. Analysis of OAC whole genomes confirmed the early-life origins of cancer-associated CNAs. The malignant transformation potential of BO may be set during the first decades of life, enabling early cancer interception.

papers.title: Sedatives reduce human gastric slow-wave amplitude, assessed by a multicenter study of endoscopic gastric mapping
papers.abstract: BackgroundGastrointestinal (GI) motility disorders are prevalent, impose a significant burden, and are associated with disrupted spatial propagation of bioelectrical gastric slow waves. High-resolution endoscopic gastric mapping (EGM) is an emerging minimally invasive technique for imaging gastric electrical activity; however, EGM is performed alongside standard gastroscopy and requires procedural sedation, which may interact with gastric electrical activity, distorting clinical insights. This study explored the influence of procedural sedation on EGM-recorded slow-wave activity. MethodsEGM was performed for [~]7 min in 32 patients undergoing upper GI endoscopy at two New Zealand hospitals. Endoscopists administered procedural sedation (fentanyl and midazolam) according to best clinical practice. The relationship between slow-wave amplitude and patient characteristics was then investigated using a variety of statistical techniques. Key ResultsGastric slow waves were detected in 30 of 32 patients who underwent EGM. Symptom scores and demographic measures were comparable between sites. Fentanyl (A, 93.4 {+/-} 13.7 g vs B, 137.5 {+/-} 33.7 g, p[≤]0.001) and midazolam (A, 5.0 {+/-} 0.9 mg vs B, 7.4 {+/-} 1.6 mg, p[≤]0.001) doses were higher at Hospital B than Hospital A. Correspondingly, slow-wave amplitudes were lower at Hospital B than Hospital A (A, 2.33 {+/-} 1.61 mV vs B, 0.86 {+/-} 1.01 mV, p=0.004). All other slow-wave metrics were consistent between hospitals. Combined sedative dose was negatively correlated with slow-wave amplitude (p=0.037). Conclusions & InferencesHigher procedural sedative doses are associated with lower-amplitude gastric slow-waves. Procedural sedation dose and opiate administration should be carefully considered when interpreting GI electrophysiology measurements.

papers.title: Serum proteins predict incident inflammatory bowel disease 14 years before diagnosis: a machine-learning and Cox modelling in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: Using an analysis pipeline that combines machine learning-based feature selection with classical statistical modelling, we aimed to predict incident inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and to identify candidate proteins associated with disease development. We used UK Biobank data in an observational cohort study of 52,331 participants with proteomics data and without a history of IBD. The cohort was split into an 80/20 train/test dataset, and three separate extreme gradient boosting models were trained on the training dataset. Using Shapley values, we ranked the predictive importance of 2,912 proteins for incident IBD, Crohns disease (CD), and ulcerative colitis (UC). The top 20 proteins per outcome served as features in multivariate Cox models predicting 350 incident cases over 14 years. All three proteomics Cox models showed moderate discrimination in the test dataset, with the UC model performing the best (C-index: 0.68), followed by IBD (C-index: 0.65), and CD (C-index: 0.60). All proteomics models outperformed clinical models. Smoking remained the only significant clinical predictor in the combined proteomics + clinical model. 48 unique proteins were identified across the three models, with 16 reaching statistical significance (p< 0.05). Machine learning-based feature selection with statistical survival modelling identifies plasma proteins that predict incident IBD and highlight biologically plausible, potentially targetable pathways in the preclinical phase of IBD.

papers.title: Replacing animal-sourced with plant-sourced proteins alters gut microbiota and biomarkers associated with colorectal cancer risk in healthy adults: A randomized feeding study
papers.abstract: Epidemiological studies associate replacing animal-sourced with plant-sourced protein with lower colorectal cancer (CRC) risk, but controlled feeding studies have rarely tested how this substitution alters the gut microbiota and CRC-related biomarkers. In a 12-week randomized controlled feeding study, 136 healthy adults consumed diets providing 30 energy percent (E%), 50 E%, or 70 E% of protein from plant sources. Change in gut microbiota composition was the primary outcome; stool characteristics, fecal N-nitroso compounds (NOCs), and fecal and plasma bile acids (BAs) were secondary outcomes. The 70% plant-protein diet significantly restructured the gut microbiota, increasing fiber-associated Lachnospiraceae and Roseburia while reducing Methanobrevibacter and several asaccharolytic taxa. Microbial functional potential shifted toward plant-carbohydrate degradation, with lower amino acid degradation and methanogenesis. Fecal pH decreased, stool characteristics suggested faster colonic transit, and potentially carcinogenic total and haem-derived NOCs declined progressively with plant-protein replacement. The 70% plant-protein diet also reduced fecal secondary and taurine-conjugated BAs, including the CRC-associated BAs DCA and LCA. Plasma glucuronidated BAs increased, expanding the circulating pool of readily excreted BA conjugates. Higher insoluble fiber intake was associated with greater microbiota restructuring and lower fecal NOCs. Methanogen carriers had higher baseline fecal NOCs and features of slower colonic transit, and showed weaker microbiota and less favorable BA responses to the 70% plant-protein diet. Baseline methanogen carriage thus could be exploited for participant stratification in future dietary interventions. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03206827.

papers.title: Disrupted microbial queuosine biosynthesis contributes to dysbiosis of human inflammatory bowel disease
papers.abstract: Background and AimsAs a microbiome/diet-derived vitamin, queuine (q) is a micronutrient that eukaryotes acquire from microbiota or diet. Vitamin q, the free base form of queuosine (Q), is used for Q-modification of transfer RNA (tRNA). Although tRNA-Q-modification in regulating eukaryotic cell physiology is recognized, the relationship between Q-tRNA-modification and the human microbiome in health and inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) remains unknown. Which bacteria produce q and how the q-producing bacteria contributing to human health and IBD are not explored. Here, we hypothesize that disrupted microbial Q-biosynthesis contributes to the dysbiosis of human IBD. We performed comprehensive multi-omics integrative analyses using publicly available datasets. Specifically, we re-analyzed publicly available shotgun metagenomic, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), metabolic datasets, and completed meta-analysis. MethodsTo systematically investigate microbial Q-biosynthesis in healthy individuals and IBD patients, we performed a systematic secondary analysis by integrating 9 publicly available metagenomic datasets, 15 scRNA-seq datasets and one metabolic dataset published prior to 2026. We present a novel secondary bioinformatic reanalysis of sequence outputs mapped to the latest microbial taxonomy, functional pathways and microbial Q-related genes. Longitudinal study of shotgun metagenomics across the human lifespan (3146 samples) enabled taxonomic and functional profiling. ResultsWe first identified key q-producing bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides and Alistipes) in healthy populations. We then found that patients with IBD had significantly reducation of q-producing bacteria and a coordinated downregulation of the Q-related pathways, including Q, preQ0, de novo guanosine ribonucleotide biosynthesis and de novo guanosine deoxyribonucleotide biosynthesis pathways. This functional impairment was primarily driven by reduced contributions from Bacteroides, Alistipes and Akkermansia. The longitudinal stability of the q-producing bacteria community across the human lifespan (1638 samples). We observed a significant negative correlation between host age and the abundance of q-producing bacteria in patients with UC. Moreover, Queuine tRNA-ribosyltransferase 1 (QTRT1) expression in human intestinal epithelial cells was significantly reduced in patients with IBD compared to healthy controls. ConclusionsOur study used multi-omics datasets to define a novel functional dysbiosis characterized by a reduction of microbial Q-biosynthesis in patients with IBD. Vitamin q and its tRNA modification is lesser-recognized in human IBD. Understanding the cellular and organismal mechanisms of this microbiome-dependent micronutrient will advance the prevention of IBD and improve the quality of life of patients with IBD. What is already known on this topic?Queuine, vitamin q, is a highly conserved hypermodified nucleoside micronutrition could only be acquired from microbiota or diet. It is used for modification of transfer RNA to protein transitional fidelity, but the specific microbial pathways evolved and the relationship with IBD are unclear. What this study addsThis study identifies a novel functional dysbiosis in IBD patients characterized by the depletion of q-producing gut bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides and Alistipes) and the downregulated microbial Q biosynthesis pathways, which correlates with host QTRT1 deficiency to potentially drive IBD pathogenesis. How this study might affect research, practice or policyO_LI1. Identifies the altered Q-biosynthesis pathway in human IBD. Establishes the "Microbial Q-synthesis-Host tRNA modification" axis as a novel mechanistic link, shifting human IBD microbiome research from taxonomic description to functional epitranscriptomics. C_LIO_LIOvercomes the inherent biases of traditional meta-analyses through a unified secondary bioinformatic reanalysis, leveraging HMP unified metabolic analysis network 3 (HUMAnN3)-based modeling of 3,000+ samples, to reveal a universal breakdown of the microbial Q-biosynthetic supply chain across all IBD subtypes. C_LIO_LIRecognize vitamin q as a critical gut-health micronutrient, influencing dietary guidelines and the regulation of functional medical foods for IBD management. C_LI

papers.title: METABOLIC DYSFUNCTION-ASSOCIATED STEATOTIC LIVER DISEASE IN PATIENTS WITH INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE: ASSOCIATION WITH BODY MASS INDEX AND DISEASE SEVERITY
papers.abstract: Whether body mass index (BMI) can meaningfully distinguish inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients with concomitant metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) was examined in a retrospective hospital series. The analysis covered 400 records from 2023-2024 with verified ulcerative colitis or Crohns disease and sufficient information on anthropometry, liver status, and intestinal disease activity. Normal BMI was documented in 118 patients, 176 were overweight, and 106 had obesity. MASLD classification required documented hepatic steatosis in the appropriate cardiometabolic setting; ultrasonography provided the principal evidence of steatosis, while laboratory findings, non-invasive indices, and elastography were considered when available. Ulcerative colitis activity was based on the Mayo Score and Crohns disease activity on CDAI. Overall, 181 patients (45.3%) met MASLD criteria. The corresponding frequencies across the three BMI strata were 20.3%, 49.4%, and 66.0% ({chi}2=49.29; p<0.001). Severe IBD was recorded in 6.8%, 14.8%, and 32.1%, respectively ({chi}2=39.45; p<0.001). Relative to normal BMI, the unadjusted odds of MASLD were 3.83-fold higher with overweight (95% CI 2.24-6.55) and 7.62-fold higher with obesity (95% CI 4.17-13.91). Thus, BMI categories identified groups with distinctly different burdens of both MASLD and severe IBD. Because treatment exposure, disease duration, and other covariates were not included in an adjusted model, the observed differences should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

papers.title: Prediction of incident inflammatory bowel disease from routine electronic health records: development and external validation of a longitudinal machine learning model
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMSInflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is often diagnosed months to years after symptoms begin, and diagnostic delay is associated with complications. We tested whether longitudinal machine learning using electronic health record (EHR) data can identify incident IBD before diagnosis, and quantified lead time and deployment burden. METHODSWe studied adults with an IBD-compatible symptom, sign, or finding at UCSF (2012-2024). Incident cases were confirmed by structured filtering and validated large language model note review. We trained a state space model (Mamba) and comparators on pre-diagnostic EHR data, excluding diagnostic-workup features, and assessed discrimination at 6- and 12-month landmarks. We externally tested Mamba without recalibration at ZSFG, a safety-net hospital serving a demographically and socioeconomically distinct population, and simulated diagnosis-code-only deployment at UCSF. RESULTSSix months after presentation, among patients still undiagnosed (67% of UCSF test cases), Mamba achieved an AUROC of 0.969 (95% CI, 0.928-0.999) at UCSF and 0.965 (0.952-0.976) at ZSFG. Median lead time was 20 months at UCSF and 15 months at ZSFG. Among future cases with an initially normal colonoscopy (N=32) or a histological finding of acute inflammation without chronicity (N=63), the model flagged 84% and 89% of these patients, respectively, before those procedures, indicating the potential for pre-diagnostic detection. Among 358,886 symptomatic patients not used for training (60 incident cases), the diagnosis-code-only model achieved an AUROC of 0.926; reviewing 20 alerts/month identified 34 cases (PPV, 1.09%; 64-fold above baseline). CONCLUSIONSLongitudinal machine learning can identify increased IBD risk months to years before diagnosis and may define a population for prospective studies of early IBD biology. Prospective evaluation should determine whether earlier identification reduces diagnostic delay. What You Need to KnowO_ST_ABSBackground and ContextC_ST_ABSIBD is often diagnosed months to years after symptoms begin. Whether routinely collected electronic health record data can identify future IBD before diagnosis, and at what alert burden, is unknown. New FindingsA longitudinal model identified future IBD six months after first symptomatic presentation with an AUROC of 0.97 and a median lead time of 20 months, with similar external discrimination. LimitationsThis was a retrospective study; external case labels were inferred rather than adjudicated, and colonoscopy analyses were exploratory. Whether earlier flagging shortens time to diagnosis requires prospective evaluation. Clinical Research RelevanceRoutinely collected structured EHR data could support targeted gastroenterology review of recurrently symptomatic patients. Because incident IBD is rare among symptomatic patients, a service reviewing 20 flagged charts per month would identify roughly one future case every five months. Deployment should therefore begin in silent mode, with locally calibrated thresholds and prospective measurement of alert burden. Basic Research RelevanceThe model flagged most future cases before a pre-diagnostic colonoscopy read as normal, or before biopsies showing only acute inflammation. Patients flagged despite normal-appearing mucosa may represent a preclinical population in which the earliest immunologic, serologic, and microbial events of IBD could be studied prospectively, including through model-guided mucosal sampling. Lay SummaryAn AI system reviewing medical records data is able to identify people who would later be diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease, often more than a year before doctors made the diagnosis.

papers.title: Longitudinal multi-omics profiling of tofacitinib response identifies a pre-existing Janus kinase-tractable inflammatory state in ulcerative colitis
papers.abstract: BO_SCPLOWACKGROUNDC_SCPLOWO_SCPCAP C_SCPCAP& OO_SCPLOWBJECTIVEC_SCPLOWTofacitinib, a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor, is approved for ulcerative colitis (UC). We investigated baseline and longitudinal transcriptomics and proteomics in intestinal biopsies, peripheral blood, and serum from UC patients starting tofacitinib to characterize treatment-associated effects and identify which molecular compartment harbors the most predictive response-associated biomarkers. MO_SCPLOWETHODSC_SCPLOWIn this prospective, open-label study, patients with moderately to severely active UC started tofacitinib 10 mg BID for eight weeks. Clinical, biochemical, endoscopic, and histological data were collected at baseline and week 8. The primary outcome, histo-endoscopic mucosal improvement (HEMI), was defined as endoscopic Mayo subscore [≤]1 with histologic remission (Robarts Histopathology Index [≤]3, no mucosal neutrophils). Mucosal biopsies and peripheral blood were collected at baseline and week 8 for bulk RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq); biopsies and serum underwent proteomic profiling using Olink Explore 384 (Cardiometabolic, Inflammation, Neurology, Oncology panels). RO_SCPLOWESULTSC_SCPLOWIn total, 127 paired multi-omic samples were collected longitudinally from 40 UC patients: 15 (38%) achieved HEMI at week 8 (responders), 13 (32.5%) were late responders, and 12 (30%) were non-responders. Pretreatment mucosal biopsies from future responders showed elevated interferon, IL-6-family, IL-2/common-{gamma}-chain, and T-cell-receptor signaling gene expression, which declined on treatment only in responders. A responder-specific JAK-STAT-dependent mechanism spanned interferon, cytokine-receptor, T-cell-receptor, and NF-{kappa}B signaling, with concordant gene- and protein-level reductions. Compared with a public infliximab dataset, JAK-STAT/interferon downregulation was shared and response-independent, while non-canonical NF-{kappa}B downregulation was tofacitinib-specific. In blood, shared pathway labels reflected distinct genes from mucosal effectors. CO_SCPLOWONCLUSIONC_SCPLOWResponse to tofacitinib depends on a JAK-tractable mucosal pathway absent in non-responders, suggesting a pretreatment biomarker for predicting treatment response. What is already known on this topicPrior studies have individually interrogated transcriptomic and/or epigenomic signatures of tofacitinib response as a single modality. What this study addsOur study provides simultaneous profiling of both the transcriptome and proteome across paired mucosal and systemic compartments in patients, comparing responders with non-responders at baseline and over time. Our data support a model where tofacitinib response in UC depends on a JAK-dependent pro-inflammatory phenotype that the drug can dismantle, in contrast to non-responders representing distinct, JAK-independent pathways. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThis study provides a foundation for treatment response studies in UC towards the development and validation of predictive biomarkers in colonic mucosa and blood, which could ultimately result in more personalized treatment strategies.

papers.title: Machine learning predicts relapse after anti-TNF withdrawal in ulcerative colitis using rectal biopsy transcriptomics
papers.abstract: BackgroundThere are currently no available biomarkers that predict the clinical outcome of ulcerative colitis (UC) patients after anti-TNF withdrawal. Here we developed a semi-supervised machine learning framework on RNA-seq data derived from rectal biopsies to predict relapse following anti-TNF discontinuation. MethodsWe included UC patients (n=136) enrolled in the prospective, randomized controlled BIOSTOP trial. Patients were assigned to a withdrawal group (stopped treatment immediately) or a maintenance group (stopped treatment after 2 years). A machine learning framework was trained on gene expression data from mucosal biopsies collected at baseline from the withdrawal group and validated in the maintenance group using baseline samples (test cohort) and 2-year follow-up samples (interference cohort). ResultsA semi-supervised machine learning model, combining a shared UMAP manifold representation with LabelSpreading on a targeted 38-gene panel achieved an AUC of 0.794, a sensitivity of 90.3%, and a specificity of 73.1% on the test cohort, and an AUC of 0.711, a sensitivity of 82.9%, and a specificity of 42.3% on the inference cohort. Applying Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) we found that IL1B, TYROBP, REG1B, S100A8, and TNF showed the highest predictive importance for relapse risk, whereas MUC2, HMGCS2, and CDKN1A displayed the highest predictive importance for sustained remission. ConclusionThe high sensitivity makes the model a promising screening tool to prevent withdrawal-related relapse, though its moderate specificity underscores the need for multi-center validation in larger, more diverse cohorts before clinical deployment.

papers.title: Integrated single-cell and proteomic profiling of pancreatic neoplasia identifies tissue markers that outperform established diagnostic markers in distinguishing cancer from precursor lesions.
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) arises within an extensively remodeled microenvironment, yet tissue markers that distinguish invasive carcinoma from precursor lesions remain limited. Integrating four single-cell RNA-sequencing atlases comprising 324,662 cells from 26 patients, we identified cancer-associated fibroblast expansion, accumulation of C1QA+ immunoregulatory macrophages, and depletion of a dendritic-cell compartment expressing plasmacytoid markers. Fibroblasts were enriched for extracellular-matrix and PI3K-AKT programs and macrophages for an antigen-presentation program. We then examined the protein-level correlates of these populations in a tissue proteomic reference framework of 356 samples spanning non-diseased pancreas, normal-adjacent tissue, low- and high-grade intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), IPMN-associated invasive carcinoma, and PDAC, prioritizing proteins that changed monotonically across the six histopathologic reference groups or marked tumor-enriched cell types. Despite depletion of plasmacytoid dendritic cells, the principal source of type I interferon, the interferon-stimulated protein ISG15, expressed by both fibroblasts and macrophages, increased monotonically toward PDAC. In exploratory cross-validated benchmarking of PDAC versus low- and high-grade IPMN, excluding IPMN-associated invasive carcinoma (145 versus 56 samples), CATB+EPIPL achieved an AUC of 0.98, with a sensitivity of 92% at an achieved specificity of 92%, exceeding protein-abundance models of diagnostic IHC-associated markers (S100P+IMP3+maspin+MSLN, 0.79) and refitted published IPMN-progression combinations ([≤]0.91). Against non-diseased pancreas, candidate and comparator panels performed similarly (AUC 0.99-1.00). These biologically informed tissue protein panels warrant independent validation, including immunohistochemical evaluation of EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy specimens and measurement in blood.
